data.author: Jasmine Pennic
data.full_text:
Talkiatry Scales Employed Therapy Nationwide Across 50 States and 170M Lives

What You Should Know Leading virtual behavioral health group Talkiatry announced the nationwide expansion of its psychotherapy services, making coordinated, in-network therapy available alongside psychiatric care across all 50 U.S. states.

Reinforces its clinical scale as the nation’s largest private employer of psychiatrists: directly employs over 400 full-time therapists alongside more than 800 full-time psychiatrists, avoiding 1099 contractor gig models to drive clinical collaboration and care continuity.

High multi-state credentialing density: 85% of Talkiatry’s employed therapists hold active clinical licenses across multiple states, resolving post-pandemic cross-border licensing friction for patients who relocate, travel, or commute across state lines. Capital and Partnership Acceleration: From $210M Series D to AMGA Network Integration The nationwide therapy rollout represents the operational execution of a massive growth phase fueled by Talkiatry’s $210M Series D financing round closed earlier this year (led by Perceptive Advisors). That round bolstered Talkiatry’s balance sheet to advance AI-supported clinical operations and build out a full-stack, multimodal care delivery organization. Simultaneously, the expansion capitalizes on Talkiatry’s nationwide partnership with the American Medical Group Association (AMGA)—whose member health systems and multispecialty medical groups deliver care to one in three Americans. By functioning as the preferred in-network outpatient behavioral health partner for more than 70 major health systems (and nearly a third of the top 20 health systems nationally), Talkiatry provides hospital networks and accountable care organizations (ACOs) with a direct, zero-cost referral destination that eliminates behavioral health boarding in emergency departments and primary care suites. To date, the company has surpassed 4 million completed patient visits—accelerating past the 3 million mark reported earlier in 2026—while maintaining in-network commercial payer contracts covering more than 170 million lives across more than 100 insurers. The Clinical Architecture: Collaborative Practice Drives Retention and Outcomes Unlike 1099 contractor marketplaces that treat therapy and psychiatry as unbundled, transactional commodities, Talkiatry utilizes an integrated, full-time employment model: Synchronized Interdisciplinary Care Teams: Psychiatrists and psychotherapists share a unified electronic health record and proprietary AI-driven clinical workflow platform. Therapists can flag medication side effects, treatment non-adherence, or emerging crises directly to the treating psychiatrist, while psychiatrists can reinforce specific cognitive-behavioral tools during monthly medication check-ins.

Psychiatrists and psychotherapists share a unified electronic health record and proprietary AI-driven clinical workflow platform. Therapists can flag medication side effects, treatment non-adherence, or emerging crises directly to the treating psychiatrist, while psychiatrists can reinforce specific cognitive-behavioral tools during monthly medication check-ins. Doubling Patient Retention: The clinical return of this unified approach is immediate: Talkiatry reports that patients who see both a Talkiatry therapist and psychiatrist maintain their connection to care two times longer than those receiving psychiatric medication management alone.

Rapid Therapeutic Alliance: Internal clinical quality measurements reveal that nearly 85% of Talkiatry therapists establish a positive therapeutic relationship within the first 30 days of treatment, directly addressing the high early-stage drop-off rates common in virtual behavioral health platforms.

Payer-Validated Health Economics: In prior payer cohort analyses of Talkiatry patients managing anxiety and depression, the coordinated model demonstrated a 68% reduction in psychiatric hospitalizations, a 32% drop in emergency department visits, and an estimated $700 net medical cost savings per member per month. Dr. Georgia Gaveras, Co-founder and Chief Medical Officer of Talkiatry, highlighted the systemic friction: “Telehealth made mental healthcare more accessible almost overnight, but it also created a patchwork of quick fixes. Multistate licensure has become a moving target since the pandemic, and it’s created real inconsistency for patients who move, travel, or live near a state line. What patients need is centralized, high-quality care across the full spectrum of mental healthcare – psychiatrists and therapists working collaboratively, leading to the best care outcomes possible. This expansion of our therapy offering nationwide enables a more coordinated behavioral health experience for patients and clinicians.”

data.title: Talkiatry Expands Therapy Nationwide, Now Available Alongside Psychiatric Care in All 50 States
data.ai_summary: Talkiatry announced its therapy services are now available in all 50 states, with over 400 therapists and 800+ psychiatrists. The company has delivered over 4 million patient visits and serves more than 170 million covered lives. The expansion aims to provide coordinated behavioral health care across the acuity spectrum.

industries.name: General Mental Health Therapy Platforms (Talk Therapy)

data.full_text:
With more than 400 therapists credentialed across the country, working in tandem with the company's 800+ full-time psychiatrists, Talkiatry spans more than 100 insurers, covers over 170 million lives, and has delivered over 4 million patient visits NEW YORK, Oct. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Talkiatry, the nation's largest private employer of psychiatrists and the preferred in-network psychiatry partner for more than 70 U.S. health systems, today announced that its therapy services are now available in all 50 states. The company now directly employs over 400 therapists, 85% of whom are licensed in multiple states, enabling consistent access to care for Talkiatry's more than 170 million covered lives nationwide. Following Talkiatry's partnership with AMGA (American Medical Group Association) to expand access to in-network psychiatric care nationwide and the company's $210M Series D funding round earlier this year, this expansion marks the next step toward Talkiatry's vision of providing comprehensive behavioral health care across the acuity spectrum, from low to high. "Telehealth made mental healthcare more accessible almost overnight, but it also created a patchwork of quick fixes," said Dr. Georgia Gaveras, co-founder and Chief Medical Officer of Talkiatry. "Multistate licensure has become a moving target since the pandemic, and it's created real inconsistency for patients who move, travel, or live near a state line. What patients need is centralized, high-quality care across the full spectrum of mental healthcare – psychiatrists and therapists working collaboratively, leading to the best care outcomes possible. This expansion of our therapy offering nationwide enables a more coordinated behavioral health experience for patients and clinicians." Fragmented care remains one of the biggest barriers to effective mental healthcare. Nationally, only around 50% of the nearly 60 million adults with a mental illness receive treatment in a given year. In the U.S., the average wait time to receive behavioral health services is 48 days. For patients who do receive care, many see a therapist and psychiatrist through separate provider networks, with little to no communication between the two. Talkiatry's model is designed to close that gap, with therapy utilized as a targeted tool psychiatrists and care teams can leverage alongside medication management to support patients in improving mental health outcomes. Talkiatry has demonstrated the impact of this model. Patients who see both a Talkiatry therapist and psychiatrist maintain their connection to care two times longer than those receiving psychiatric care alone. Additionally, nearly 85% of Talkiatry therapists build a positive therapeutic relationship with their patients within the first month of care, based on the company's clinical quality measurement. Talkiatry's approach is designed to deliver a more connected care experience by bringing psychiatry and therapy together under one coordinated care team. The company has now delivered 4 million visits, surpassing the 3 million mark announced earlier this year. With this continued momentum, Talkiatry is making a broader range of mental health services available to every patient throughout their mental health journey. "Patients often come to us after bouncing between a therapist and a psychiatrist who've never spoken. That disconnect is where care falls through the cracks," said David Guggenheim, National Director of Psychotherapy at Talkiatry. "Being able to expand our coordinated model into therapy nationwide means offering every patient a consistent care experience from the start of their mental health journey." Talkiatry's therapy expansion applies the same full-time clinician model that has allowed the company to become the nation's largest private employer of psychiatrists. By employing clinicians full-time, Talkiatry empowers providers to build meaningful, long-term relationships with patients, while fostering greater continuity and collaboration across care teams. This approach has solidified Talkiatry as a trusted partner for health systems, payers, and referring physicians across the care continuum. To learn more about Talkiatry's therapy services, visit talkiatry.com. About Talkiatry Talkiatry is a full-stack provider group delivering in-network psychiatric and therapy care across the United States. The company directly employs more than 800 full-time psychiatrists, making it the largest private employer of psychiatrists in the country, and has delivered 4 million patient visits to date. Talkiatry serves as the preferred psychiatry partner for health systems, payers, and employers seeking dependable access and superior outcomes. The company's care model is underpinned by proprietary AI-powered technology to manage care delivery, streamline clinical operations, and engage members. Talkiatry was co-founded by Robert Krayn and Georgia Gaveras, DO. Learn more at talkiatry.com and follow us on LinkedIn, Facebook, and Instagram. Media Contact

data.title: Talkiatry takes therapy nationwide as it builds out behavioral health platform
data.ai_summary: Talkiatry is expanding virtual therapy services nationwide, offering therapy in all 50 states with over 400 directly employed therapists. The company, which employs 800+ psychiatrists, has raised $400 million and plans to pilot an Intensive Outpatient Program. It aims to coordinate care between psychiatrists and therapists, addressing fragmented mental health access.
data.author: Heather Landi

industries.name: General Mental Health Therapy Platforms (Talk Therapy)

data.full_text: Talkiatry is expanding virtual therapy services nationwide as part of a broader push to provide comprehensive behavioral health services across the acuity spectrum, from low to high. As a national mental health practice that provides in-network psychiatry and therapy, the expansion also positions the company to offer broader behavioral health services to health systems, payers and employers. The company initially built its scale around telepsychiatry, with more than 800 employed psychiatrists and a large national insurance footprint. Talkiatry claims to be the nation’s largest private employer of psychiatrists along with the preferred in-network psychiatry partner for more than 70 U.S. health systems. The company now offers therapy services in all 50 states as it directly employs more than 400 therapists, 85% of whom are licensed in multiple states, according to the company. Talkiatry spans more than 100 insurers, covers over 170 million lives and has delivered over 4 million patient visits. The expansion of Talkiatry’s therapy offering enables a more coordinated behavioral health experience for patients and clinicians, according to Georgia Gaveras, M.D., co-founder and chief medical officer of Talkiatry. Gaveras, a practicing psychiatrist for more than 18 years, is triple board-certified in child and adolescent psychiatry, adult psychiatry, and addiction medicine. Psychiatrists often struggle to refer patients to in-network therapists and coordinate care across dozens of outside providers. By employing therapists within the same system, psychiatrists and therapists can share notes and communicate directly, creating a more seamless experience for patients, Gaveras noted. “If you have providers in the same ecosystem, the Talkiatry ecosystem, that can provide therapy and medication management, then all of a sudden it makes it a lot easier to coordinate care,” she noted. Telehealth made mental healthcare more accessible, but it also created a patchwork of "quick fixes," Gaveras noted. "Multistate licensure has become a moving target since the pandemic, and it's created real inconsistency for patients who move, travel, or live near a state line. What patients need is centralized, high-quality care across the full spectrum of mental healthcare – psychiatrists and therapists working collaboratively, leading to the best care outcomes possible," she said. Related Talkiatry closes $210M series D to expand telepsychiatry services Nationally, only around 50% of the nearly 60 million adults with a mental illness receive treatment in a given year, according to data from the National Institute of Mental Health. In the U.S., the average wait time to receive behavioral health services is 48 days. For patients who do receive care, many see a therapist and psychiatrist through separate provider networks, with little to no communication between the two. Talkiatry's model is designed to close that gap, with therapy utilized as a targeted tool psychiatrists and care teams can leverage alongside medication management to support patients in improving mental health outcomes, according to executives. Gaveras and Robert Krayn founded Talkiatry in 2020 to address the challenges patients and psychiatrists face in accessing and delivering high-quality mental healthcare. Currently, Talkiatry provides psychiatry and therapy services for a range of mental health conditions including anxiety, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, bipolar disorder, mood disorder, insomnia and post-traumatic stress disorder, among others. In February, Talkiatry, named to Fierce Healthcare’s Fierce 15 in 2024, picked up $210 million in series D funding to expand its offerings and build out its technology. The company has raised $400 million to date. In April, the company inked a partnership with AMGA (American Medical Group Association) to expand access to in-network psychiatric care for medical groups and their patients. Health systems and medical practices are seeing greater demand for mental health services as the U.S. also faces a profound shortage of behavioral health professionals. About 137 million Americans, or 40% of the U.S. population, live in federally designated Mental Health Professional Shortage Areas (HPSAs), according to Health Resources and Services Administration data. HRSA also projects the supply of psychiatrists will shrink by roughly 20% by 2030. "Health systems know that no matter what, no one entity can completely fill the need for a community. We're not replacing anything; we're complementing them. We're supplementing what it is that they need to make sure that their patients get timely access to care. And, they want to partner with a high-quality provider because if you're going to refer out to a different system for a doctor, you want to make sure that you trust where you're referring," Gaveras said. The company has expanded into group therapy and plans to pilot an Intensive Outpatient Program. Talkiatry is also exploring specialty areas such as substance use treatment, Gaveras said. The company's care model is underpinned by proprietary AI-powered technology to manage care delivery, streamline clinical operations and engage members. Talkiatry focuses on using AI to improve the experience for patients and doctors, such as deploying AI scribes for note-taking, Gaveras noted. Talkiatry points to its outcomes data as evidence of the model's impact. Patients who see both a Talkiatry therapist and psychiatrist maintain their connection to care two times longer than those receiving psychiatric care alone, according to executives. Nearly 85% of Talkiatry therapists build a positive therapeutic relationship with their patients within the first month of care, based on the company’s clinical quality measurement. A study of Talkiatry patients found that patients treated through its fully virtual psychiatry model experienced substantial reductions in depression and anxiety symptoms over roughly three months of treatment. Among patients who started with moderate-to-severe symptoms, treatment led to an average reduction of 46% for anxiety symptoms and 45% for depressive symptoms. Additionally, a peer-reviewed study found that Talkiatry's early dropout rate is up to 60% lower than industry benchmarks. "Patients often come to us after bouncing between a therapist and a psychiatrist who've never spoken. That disconnect is where care falls through the cracks," David Guggenheim, national director of psychotherapy at Talkiatry, said in a statement. "Being able to expand our coordinated model into therapy nationwide means offering every patient a consistent care experience from the start of their mental health journey." Challenges with the mental healthcare system create both access problems and economic headwinds. Patients with untreated mental health conditions often end up in the emergency department (ED), which adds up to billions in avoidable and preventable mental health ED visits each year. A 2024 National Bureau of Economic Research study estimated that untreated or undertreated mental illness costs the U.S. about $282 billion per year through lost work and reduced economic participation alone. The Mental Health TALK SAFE Act of 2025, legislation introduced in Congress this year, aims to expand access to high-quality psychiatric care through telemedicine while strengthening patient safety and accountability in telemedicine. In a commentary published in September in the American Journal of Managed Care, Jesse Ehrenfeld, M.D., past president of the American Medical Association, urged Congress to advance the legislation, arguing that it will expand telepsychiatry access by establishing permanent telehealth prescribing and licensing rules.

data.title: How CEE mental health startups are closing the care gap
data.ai_summary: CEE mental health startups are developing AI tools for clinicians and online therapy, with several expanding internationally. Funding is consolidating around insurer- or employer-paid businesses, while AI therapy faces safety and regulatory hurdles. Public reimbursement routes like Czechia's pilot and Germany's DiGA are emerging.
data.author: Katarzyna Groszkowska

industries.name: General Mental Health Therapy Platforms (Talk Therapy)

sic_codes.name: SERVICES-OFFICES & CLINICS OF DOCTORS OF MEDICINE

data.full_text:
October 8, 2026 · 8 min read Katarzyna Groszkowska Editor, Vestbee Insights How CEE mental health startups are closing the care gap Key takeaways: CEE mental health startups and AI therapy in 2026 Mental health tech is shifting from consumer apps to clinical infrastructure. The strongest models increasingly help therapists with documentation, triage, and practice management.

The strongest models increasingly help therapists with documentation, triage, and practice management. AI therapy is attracting users and investors, but safety and clinical evidence remain major hurdles. Studies of generative AI therapy show promising early results. But harmful chatbot interactions and growing regulatory scrutiny highlight the limits of replacing human therapists.

Studies of generative AI therapy show promising early results. But harmful chatbot interactions and growing regulatory scrutiny highlight the limits of replacing human therapists. Mental health funding is consolidating around fewer, larger companies. In the US and Europe, investors are favouring businesses with insurer, employer, or healthcare-system revenue over consumer subscription models.

In the US and Europe, investors are favouring businesses with insurer, employer, or healthcare-system revenue over consumer subscription models. CEE mental health startups remain underfunded despite rising demand. CEE is producing companies across AI-powered tools for clinicians, online therapy, digital therapeutics, and mental health wearables, with several expanding internationally.

CEE is producing companies across AI-powered tools for clinicians, online therapy, digital therapeutics, and mental health wearables, with several expanding internationally. Regulation and reimbursement are becoming key competitive advantages. From Czechia's new digital therapy reimbursement routes to Germany's DiGA system, access to public healthcare funding increasingly depends on clinical evidence and regulatory compliance. Demand for mental health care continues to grow, yet many people still lack access to affordable and effective support. And while unregulated AI chatbots are not the answer, technology can play a role in making mental health care more accessible. Ahead of World Mental Health Day, we take a closer look at the mental health segment of digital health, with a particular focus on CEE. How big is the world's mental health care gap? According to WHO reports, published in September 2025, more than 1 billion people live with a mental health condition. Depression and anxiety alone cost the global economy about $1 trillion a year. An OECD report published in April 2026 estimated that more than one in five people across EU countries experienced a mental disorder in 2023. Roughly two-thirds of people needing mental healthcare lack treatment coverage. The report also projected that depression, anxiety and alcohol use disorders would cost EU health systems about €76 billion annually over 2025–2050. Startups have been trying to close this care gap for years, through approaches ranging from consumer apps and online therapy to digital therapeutics. Other products support clinicians directly, saving time on documentation and practice management, while hybrid models combine digital tools with human care. CEE mental health startups to watch in 2026 These approaches are also taking shape across Central and Eastern Europe, alongside new routes to public healthcare funding. Czechia offers one example: since 2026, therapist-led digital cognitive behavioural therapy has been covered by public health insurance under conditions including a doctor’s referral and delivery by a contracted provider. In July 2026, the country’s largest health insurer also opened a pilot reimbursement route for health technologies, inspired by Germany’s DiGA scheme. Across the region, startups are active in different parts of mental health tech, from AI tools for therapists and online therapy platforms to digital therapeutics and wellness wearables. Czech-Slovakian Upheal is building AI tools not for patients but for clinicians — taking the paperwork out of therapy. It transcribes sessions, drafts progress notes, and adds practice-management and telehealth features. In November 2024, it raised a $10 million Series A led by Headline, with Credo Ventures and Kaya VC.

Prague-based Hedepy launched as an online psychotherapy marketplace in 2020 and has since shown that in fragmented, language-specific markets, growth through M&A and a strong B2B arm can beat chasing a mega-round. In September 2025, it acquired HearMe, a Polish workplace mental health platform, adding corporate clients and operating now in nine markets.

Ukrainian founders have built some of the region's most export-minded companies. Pleso Therapy, founded in Ukraine in 2021 and now run from Warsaw, matches clients with therapists using an algorithm and sells to both individuals and employers. In February 2026, it raised $2.5 million through a convertible loan at a $30 million pre-money valuation, from investors including the ICLUB syndicate and former Kyivstar CEO Petro Chernyshov.

Public reimbursement is also possible, but it takes evidence. Poland's Prosoma develops a digital therapeutic, Living Well, that targets anxiety, depression, and PTSD in cancer patients. It is reimbursed through more than 30 selective contracts in Germany and Switzerland, with early pilots in the US, and raised Series A funding from CRB Health Tech in 2025.

Not all mental health innovation is software. Lithuania's Pulsetto, founded in 2021, makes a wearable that stimulates the vagus nerve to help with stress and sleep. In February 2025, it raised €2 million from Scalewolf to adapt the device for soldiers and first responders. These companies show how technology can support clinicians and make therapy easier to access. Alongside these approaches, people are also turning to AI chatbots for emotional support. This raises questions about whether AI can help address the care gap and what evidence is needed to establish its role. Can AI replace therapists? Europe’s care gap raises questions about whether AI could make mental health support more accessible. US research offers some early context. A Pew Research Center survey published in June 2026 found that 10% of US adults had used chatbots for emotional support or advice, rising to 20% among 18–29-year-olds. Investors in AI-first products point to the shortage of care. Forerunner Ventures, which backs AI therapy startup Slingshot AI, cites about 56 million Americans who sought therapy in 2022 against roughly 500,000 licensed behavioural health providers. Clinical evidence for AI therapy is only beginning to be evaluated. Dartmouth’s trial of Therabot, a generative AI chatbot, found that over eight weeks, participants’ depression symptoms fell by an average of 51% and anxiety symptoms by 31%. The comparison group, however, was a waiting list rather than another treatment. The researchers cautioned that “no generative AI agent is ready to operate fully autonomously in mental health” and stressed the need for clinician oversight. Alongside tools that offer support directly to patients, AI is also becoming part of professionals’ work. In a 2025 survey, 56% of US psychologists reported using AI at work, up from 29% a year earlier, including for tasks such as writing and administration. Mental health startup funding in 2026: big rounds and consolidation Mental health is still the most-funded clinical area in US digital health, a position it has held for seven consecutive years. Across the Atlantic, money goes to fewer, larger companies, mostly those paid by insurers rather than by consumers. In February 2026, psychiatry provider Talkiatry raised a $210 million Series D led by Perceptive Advisors, with a16z participating. A month later, therapy network Grow Therapy raised $150 million at a reported $3 billion valuation, led by TCV and Goldman Sachs Alternatives. European rounds remain smaller: Dutch employee mental health platform OpenUp raised €20 million in March 2026, and UK-based JAAQ raised £13 million the same month. 2026 has also been a year of consolidation: Hospital operator Universal Health Services completed its acquisition of Talkspace, an online therapy provider, in August, at an enterprise value of about $835 million. Portugal-founded Sword Health agreed to buy Headspace for a reported 300 million in cash. Why do so many mental health startups fail? These deals show that mental health can attract substantial investment. But turning demand for care into a sustainable business remains difficult, and many startups have shut down along the way. An analysis of 542 digital mental health companies, cited by EU-Startups, found that 53% of those relying on consumers to pay had shut down or gone bankrupt. Woebot, one of the best-known therapy chatbots, retired its app in June 2025 after raising $123.5 million, and its founder linked this failure to the cost of meeting FDA requirements. Another example is a voice-biomarker startup, Kintsugi, which closed in February 2026 before winning FDA clearance and open-sourced its models. Germany's Mika, an app for cancer patients with anxiety and depression, lost its place in the national app reimbursement scheme over a study registration issue, and with it, most of its revenue. Kintsugi's CEO Grace Chang summed up the tension many founders face: “Venture investors still expect you to be at $100 million in ARR by year ten — and now… by year three or five. But in healthcare, you can't even sell your commercial product until you are FDA-cleared.” Lessons for founders and investors in CEE mental health tech The companies, funding rounds, and setbacks discussed above offer practical lessons for founders and investors in CEE. Demand for mental health care is substantial, but building a sustainable business also requires a clear payment route, evidence that the product works, and enough funding to reach the market. For founders: Keep a human in the loop. Regulators, clinicians and buyers are far more comfortable with AI that supports professionals than with AI that replaces them.

Regulators, clinicians and buyers are far more comfortable with AI that supports professionals than with AI that replaces them. Plan the payment route early. Czechia's new pilot, Germany's DiGA scheme and NHS digital front doors show that reimbursement is possible, but each demands evidence.

Czechia's new pilot, Germany's DiGA scheme and NHS digital front doors show that reimbursement is possible, but each demands evidence. Design for the EU AI Act now. Transparency duties already apply, and emotion recognition at work is banned.

Transparency duties already apply, and emotion recognition at work is banned. Prepare for international growth. Upheal, Hedepy and Pleso all looked beyond their home market from the start.

Upheal, Hedepy and Pleso all looked beyond their home market from the start. Treat evidence as a moat. With research showing modest effects across the board, products that can prove outcomes will stand out. For investors: Assess the payer alongside the need. Rising sick leave, long waiting lists, and new reimbursement routes point to demand that capital has not yet matched.

Rising sick leave, long waiting lists, and new reimbursement routes point to demand that capital has not yet matched. Match funding to development timelines. Kintsugi’s experience shows how clinical research and regulatory requirements can stretch beyond investors’ expectations of rapid growth

Kintsugi’s experience shows how clinical research and regulatory requirements can stretch beyond investors’ expectations of rapid growth Consider strategic buyers as a route to an exit. Hedepy's purchase of HearMe, the sale of Czech startup VOS.health to a US company, and Sweden's Mindler buying ieso's UK business show the consolidation path.

Hedepy's purchase of HearMe, the sale of Czech startup VOS.health to a US company, and Sweden's Mindler buying ieso's UK business show the consolidation path. Regulation cuts both ways. It raises the cost of entry, as Woebot and Kintsugi found, but it also protects the companies that clear the bar. Analysis#Healthtech#Startups October 8, 2026

data.title: Talkiatry Recognized by the American Medical Association for its Dedication to Clinician Well-Being
data.ai_summary: Talkiatry, the nation's largest private employer of psychiatrists, was recognized by the American Medical Association as a Joy in Medicine organization for its clinician well-being efforts. The company supports its 800+ psychiatrists through peer support groups, listening sessions, and a well-being committee. The AMA's program has recognized over 250 organizations since 2019.

data.full_text:
Talkiatry supports its national team of 800+ psychiatrists through peer support groups, clinician listening sessions, and a formal well-being committee. NEW YORK, Oct. 8, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Talkiatry, the nation's largest private employer of psychiatrists and the preferred in-network psychiatry partner for more than 70 U.S. health systems, today announced it has earned recognition from the American Medical Association (AMA) as a Joy in Medicine® organization. The prestigious recognition from the country's leading physician association honors health systems, hospitals, and medical groups that prioritize proven methods to reduce burnout and enhance the professional fulfillment of doctors that comes from patient care. Organizations that meet the rigorous criteria of the Joy in Medicine Health System Recognition Program are leaders in the national effort to transform healthcare work systems and address the root causes of burnout among care teams. Burnout rates continue to decline, yet U.S. physicians remain at higher risk for burnout relative to other U.S. workers. Systemic drivers like administrative burden, staffing shortages and stigma around mental health continue to plague the physician experience and contribute to the day-to-day stressors facing physicians today. Continued efforts are essential to ensure doctors receive the support they need to thrive and achieve national health goals. "As a fully virtual, national psychiatry practice, we have to think differently about how we support our clinicians. Our psychiatrists don't have the same opportunities to connect informally that they might in a traditional practice. There's no shared break room or hallway conversation between shifts," said Dr. Georgia Gaveras, DO, co-founder and Chief Medical Officer of Talkiatry. "That's why we've been very intentional about building support structures into the technology and workflows our psychiatrists already use every day, and making them convenient, accessible, and effective." Talkiatry takes a multifaceted approach to clinician well-being, reflected in its workforce model, technology and dedicated support programs. The company employs its clinicians full-time, with a focus on long-term well-being, while its technology helps reduce administrative burden — a leading driver of physician burnout nationally — by automating documentation and care coordination. These efforts are complemented by programs that give clinicians opportunities to share feedback, connect with peers and access support, including: Clinician Roundtables: Small-group listening sessions where treating psychiatrists meet virtually with leadership to share feedback on the practice environment, clinical workflows and systems that shape their day-to-day work. Discussions have addressed topics including administrative support, pain points with new and evolving processes, compensation, EHR challenges, and collaboration across psychiatrists, nurse practitioners and therapists. Key themes and action areas are shared with relevant stakeholders across the organization to inform ongoing improvements.

Discussions have addressed topics including administrative support, pain points with new and evolving processes, compensation, EHR challenges, and collaboration across psychiatrists, nurse practitioners and therapists. Key themes and action areas are shared with relevant stakeholders across the organization to inform ongoing improvements. Peer Support Program: A confidential, peer-led resource that gives clinicians support when navigating difficult patient encounters, critical or adverse events, burnout or work-life balance concerns.

Clinician Well-Being Committee: Reviews findings from Talkiatry's annual clinician burnout assessment and works collaboratively to identify areas for improvement and develop recommendations for clinical leadership. "Supporting physician well-being helps create better care for everyone," said AMA President Willie Underwood III, MD, MSc, MPH. "Studies show that when physicians are supported, patients benefit from safer care, higher quality, and a better overall experience. Organizations recognized by the Joy in Medicine Program are leading the way by investing in workplaces that support physicians and help them deliver compassionate, high-quality care. The AMA is proud to honor these leaders for their commitment to physician well-being and healthier communities." Since its inception in 2019, the AMA Joy in Medicine Health System Recognition Program has recognized more than 250 organizations across the country. Recognition levels are valid for two years. This year, a total of 92 health organizations nationwide earned recognition with documented efforts to reduce system-level drivers of work-related burnout and demonstrated competencies in commitment, assessment, leadership, efficiency of practice environment, teamwork, and support. Organizations that earned 2026-2027 recognition join a strong group of currently recognized organizations from the 2025-2026 program, bringing the currently recognized cohort to 194 recognized organizations. Learn more about the AMA Joy in Medicine Health System Recognition Program at ama-assn.org/joyinmedicine. Nationally recognized Gold Seal of Approval® reflects clinical excellence behind Talkiatry's in-network psychiatric and therapy care, delivered to over 170 million covered lives nationwide NEW YORK, Oct. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Talkiatry, the nation's largest psychiatric provider group and the preferred in-network psychiatry partner for more than 70 U.S. health systems, has earned The Joint Commission's Gold Seal of Approval® for Behavioral Health. This distinction reflects Talkiatry's continued commitment to providing comprehensive, high-quality care, with more than 170 million covered lives, coming shortly after the company surpassed four million patient visits to date. Talkiatry's Joint Commission accreditation is a testament to the rigor of the provider group's processes, clinical oversight, and safety practices behind its model. The accreditation reflects Talkiatry's pursuit of clinical excellence and its focus on meeting the same clinical standards held by the country's leading brick-and-mortar healthcare institutions. As demand for behavioral healthcare continues to outpace access nationally, an increasing number of psychiatric care providers have moved to virtual and hybrid settings. With this, patients, providers, and payers have fewer ways to assess whether providers meet consistent, independently audited standards for quality and safety. The Gold Seal of Approval® is a reflection of Talkiatry's robust clinical standards and an integrated care model that brings therapy and psychiatry together to support better patient outcomes. "Earning Joint Commission accreditation is validation of our clinical infrastructure, further strengthening confidence across the board for our patients, clinicians on staff, and the providers who trust us with their patients," said Dr. Georgia Gaveras, DO, co-founder and Chief Medical Officer of Talkiatry. "We have, and continue to, invest in a clinical team that is dedicated to developing meaningful, long-term relationships with patients. Our model gives clinicians the time and resources to go beyond 15-minute intakes. At Talkiatry, the standard intake is 60 minutes, which allows our clinicians the time to truly understand their patients' needs and deliver care that is thoughtful, personalized, and clinically rigorous." This Joint Commission accreditation marks the latest milestone in a year of significant growth for Talkiatry, following the company's strategic partnership with AMGA (American Medical Group Association) to expand access to in-network psychiatric care nationwide and the company's $210M Series D funding round earlier this year. To earn the Gold Seal of Approval® for Behavioral Health, Talkiatry underwent a comprehensive review of its operations, policies, patient care delivery, and privacy and security practices to ensure compliance with Joint Commission. Surveyors from the Joint Commission then conducted on-site observations and interviews to identify performance strengths and opportunities for continued improvement before determining their final decision. "Joint Commission congratulates Talkiatry for achieving accreditation by demonstrating its focus on delivering safe and effective care of the highest quality and value," says Ken Grubbs, DNP, MBA, RN, executive vice president of Accreditation and Certification Operations and chief nursing officer, Joint Commission. "Through the accreditation process, we worked closely with Talkiatry to enable and affirm the highest standards of healthcare quality and patient safety. Together, we are elevating care for all patients, and we appreciate Talkiatry's collaboration throughout this process." About Talkiatry Talkiatry is a full-stack provider group delivering in-network psychiatric and therapy care across the United States. The company's care model is underpinned by proprietary AI-powered technology to manage care delivery, streamline clinical operations, and engage members. This expansion of our therapy offering nationwide enables a more coordinated behavioral health experience for patients and clinicians." data.full_text: The American Telemedicine Association’s virtual care advocacy group, ATA Action, has launched the new Cross-State Care Coalition, a multi-stakeholder effort to develop and advance federal legislation that would remove patient barriers to telehealth in other states. “This is not about federalizing medical licensure,” said ATA CEO Kyle Zebley, who serves as ATA Action’s executive director and will co-chair the new coalition. “It is about identifying specific circumstances where a narrow federal pathway can solve a real patient-access problem while maintaining strong safety and accountability protections,” he said in a statement on Thursday. The CSCC will convene hospitals and health systems, other provider organizations, innovators and virtual care leaders with the aim of modernizing outdated licensure rules, ATA Action said in its announcement. The goal is not to displace states’ broader authority over standards of practice, scope of practice, discipline, patient safety and professional accountability, said Zebley. “We intend to work with Republicans and Democrats, federal and state policymakers, clinicians, patient advocates and other stakeholders, and alongside our coalition members, to build support for practical legislation and get meaningful reforms signed into law,” he explained. State-based telehealth licensure creates unnecessary friction for patients and providers because duplicative requirements that do not enhance quality restrict availability, ATA Action said. “This is about building a more connected, responsive healthcare system that reflects how care is delivered today,” Zebley said. Other coalition founders include Johns Hopkins Medicine, Access TeleCare, AdventHealth, Clara, MedStar Health, The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, Sanford Health, Talkiatry and Teladoc Health; additional organizations are invited to participate. “We invite health systems, provider organizations, innovators and digital health leaders to join us in addressing this critical issue,” added Mary Fernandes, assistant director of federal strategy at Johns Hopkins University & Medicine and co-chair of the coalition, in the statement. The new coalition builds on a three-year Licensure Innovation for Telehealth Transformation (LIFTT) initiative that ATA and Johns Hopkins established earlier this year. LIFTT aims to better educate the public on what it will take to overcome state licensure hurdles and the need for federal reforms to improve telehealth across state lines. These licensure hurdles can bar patients from accessing specialty and complex subspecialty care providers, second opinions and care delivered through federally regulated clinical trials that may be unavailable in their states, ATA Action said, noting that they also hinder progress on virtual care tech. “Telehealth has expanded access and changed the way care is delivered, but licensure remains state-bound,” said Fernandes in a statement. “This initiative calls for targeted federal leadership, working alongside states, to ensure continuity of care and access to specialized services without compromising safety or accountability.” Healthcare IT News

data.full_text:
ATA Action Launches Cross-State Care Coalition to Advance Bipartisan Federal Telehealth Licensure Reform

What You Should Know ATA Action—the advocacy arm of the American Telemedicine Association (ATA)—launched the Cross-State Care Coalition, uniting health systems, digital health platforms, and clinical innovators to advance bipartisan federal legislation modernizing clinician licensure across state lines.

The coalition is co-chaired by Johns Hopkins Medicine and ATA Action, building upon policy foundations established under the Licensure Innovation for Telehealth Transformation (LIFTT) Initiative introduced in March 2026.

The legislative framework focuses on targeted, narrow federal pathways designed to reconcile conflicting state licensing rules without displacing states’ constitutional authority over clinical scope of practice, medical discipline, or patient safety standards.

The initiative targets high-friction clinical scenarios where state borders disrupt care, prioritizing established patient continuity, virtual subspecialty access, remote second opinions, rare disease management, technology-enabled care, and decentralized clinical trial protocols.

Founding healthcare health system and industry coalition members include Johns Hopkins Medicine, Access TeleCare, AdventHealth, Clara, MedStar Health, The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, Sanford Health, Talkiatry, and Teladoc Health. Preserving State Authority via Narrow Federal Exceptions A central tenet of the coalition’s policy platform is avoiding a top-down federalization of medical licensure. Instead, the initiative seeks targeted federal carve-outs that leave states’ underlying police powers, medical board disciplinary frameworks, and clinical scopes of practice intact: Narrow, Targeted Pathways: Establishes statutory safe harbors specifically where state-by-state licensing conflicts disrupt established doctor-patient relationships or restrict specialized access.

Establishes statutory safe harbors specifically where state-by-state licensing conflicts disrupt established doctor-patient relationships or restrict specialized access. Preserving State Oversight: States retain full authority over clinical standards of care, disciplinary actions, malpractice oversight, and professional accountability.

States retain full authority over clinical standards of care, disciplinary actions, malpractice oversight, and professional accountability. Non-Displacement: Rather than replacing state medical licensing compacts (such as the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact – IMLC), the federal pathways are designed to complement state reciprocity agreements. Five Core Legislative and Clinical Priorities The coalition’s policy framework focuses on high-friction clinical environments where physical borders impose acute administrative and clinical barriers: Continuity of Care for Established Patients: Enabling clinicians to provide routine follow-up, chronic condition management, and post-discharge consultations when established patients travel or temporarily cross state borders.

Enabling clinicians to provide routine follow-up, chronic condition management, and post-discharge consultations when established patients travel or temporarily cross state borders. Access to Rare, Complex, and Subspecialty Care: Permitting out-of-state tertiary and quaternary subspecialists to deliver virtual care, specialty second opinions, oncology reviews, and pre-transplant workups without requiring full redundant licensure in the patient’s home state.

Permitting out-of-state tertiary and quaternary subspecialists to deliver virtual care, specialty second opinions, oncology reviews, and pre-transplant workups without requiring full redundant licensure in the patient’s home state. Federally Regulated Clinical Trials: Removing state licensing hurdles for decentralized clinical research, enabling principal investigators and sub-investigators to monitor enrolled trial participants virtually across multiple jurisdictions.

Removing state licensing hurdles for decentralized clinical research, enabling principal investigators and sub-investigators to monitor enrolled trial participants virtually across multiple jurisdictions. Safeguarding Patient Protection & Accountability: Ensuring that every cross-state virtual consultation maintains clear lines of clinical liability, verifiable credentials, and patient safety reporting mechanisms back to state boards.

Ensuring that every cross-state virtual consultation maintains clear lines of clinical liability, verifiable credentials, and patient safety reporting mechanisms back to state boards. Interoperable, Connected Care Infrastructure: Fostering technical and policy standards that support seamless bidirectional health information exchange between out-of-state specialists and local primary care medical homes. Founding Coalition Members Across Health Systems and Digital Health The coalition unites academic medical centers, non-profit integrated delivery networks, specialty behavioral health platforms, and enterprise virtual care operators: Academic & Health System Anchors: Johns Hopkins Medicine (Co-Chair), AdventHealth, MedStar Health, The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, and Sanford Health.

Johns Hopkins Medicine (Co-Chair), AdventHealth, MedStar Health, The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, and Sanford Health. Virtual Care & Digital Health Innovators: Access TeleCare, Clara, Talkiatry, and Teladoc Health. Transitioning from Temporary Extensions to Permanent Policy The formation of the Cross-State Care Coalition marks a critical inflection point in telehealth policy. Over the past several years, virtual care advocacy largely centered on temporary legislative vehicles—such as extending Medicare telehealth flexibilities, geographic waiver suspensions, and high-deductible health plan (HDHP) safe harbors. By shifting focus toward interstate licensure, provider organizations and digital health vendors are tackling the underlying structural barrier that limits nationwide hybrid care delivery models. For multi-state health systems and virtual specialty providers, establishing narrow federal pathways provides regulatory clarity, lowers clinical compliance risk, and protects network integrity as care models evolve across state borders.

data.title: 5 Behavioral Health VC Investors to Watch
data.ai_summary: VC funding in behavioral health rebounded in 2026 after a 2024 low, with large rounds like Talkiatry's $210M Series D and Grow Therapy's $150M Series D. The article highlights five firms—GreyMatter, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Kaiser, General Catalyst, and HealthQuest—backing tech-enabled providers and specialized services.
data.author: Ashleigh Hollowell
data.full_text:
This is an exclusive BHB+ story.

Venture capital investments in behavioral health are emerging from a lull as firms recalibrated their priorities in 2024 and have since identified new strategic targets as the sector has matured.

Behavioral health, and in particular digital mental health solutions, saw an influx of capital in 2021, driven by the pandemic, with funding peaking around $4.9 billion, according to Rock Health. After that, there was talk of VC capital “drying up” around early 2022. Since then, VC funding dipped to a low of $1.4 billion in 2024. But behavioral health venture capital funding has recently been reinvigorated by investor conviction, a wave of new mental health startups and large growth funding rounds that target specialized, high-acuity services.

VC investments in behavioral health began the year with large capital rounds paid to platforms that target access and infrastructure, including a $210 million Series D round for Talkiatry, a $150 million Series D round for Grow Therapy, $80 million out of stealth for Salma Health and $40 million for AnswerNow’s telehealth applied behavioral analysis (ABA) services. All four of those mega fundraises took place during the first quarter of 2026.

Advertisement

VC investments across behavioral health during the second quarter of 2026 looked a bit different, with more attention to specialty services and slightly smaller, though still noteworthy, capital raises, including deals like Click Therapeutics’ $50 million Series D and a $30 million round for Instride Health.

Now that the market has matured past the COVID-induced telehealth arms race, venture capital funding is being prioritized for providers and solutions that have promising infrastructure and aim to improve access rather than merely investing in the promise of digital mental health.

Across all five VC firms that Behavioral Health Business is watching, one theme is clear: behavioral health is embracing technology, and the future belongs to strategic providers with scalable, tech-enabled, payer-aligned care models.

Why BHB is watching:

San Francisco-based GreyMatter Capital is a venture firm that invests solely in mental health founders. It has a swath of behavioral health providers and tech-enabled solutions in its investment portfolio, but a handful have raised significant capital to scale in the last year.

In February, virtual psychiatry provider Talkiatry raised a $210 million Series D round, which was almost the total of all the funding it had received up to that point, bringing its total funding to roughly $452 million. The company will use much of the new funding to bolster its AI capabilities.

Another one of GreyMatter’s portfolio companies, pediatric psychiatric care provider Flourish Health, raised $26 million for its Series A round in July. Its goal is to scale high-acuity psychiatric care for youth populations.

Serious mental illness provider Vanna Health secured $17 million in a Series B round earlier this summer and will use the capital to enter new markets soon. The company also named a new CEO shortly before the fundraise. One of the new CEO’s goals is to deepen payer partnerships and wraparound services for patients.

Pediatric speech, occupational and physical therapy provider Coral Care, another GreyMatter investment, secured a $13 million Series A in February, and aims to connect families with therapists for in-home services. The company noted that with this funding, it will move to scale nationally.

Other noteworthy developments among GreyMatter’s portfolio companies this year include the acquisition of Valera Health by Mindoula in July. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but Mindoula noted the deal was a move to expand its collaborative care model with established psychiatric services.

Another one we’re watching in this portfolio is Pelago’s announcement that it will transition from being historically a substance use disorder (SUD) care provider and expand into general behavioral health. Its first move in this vein was a wellness support chatbot capable of escalating issues to Pelago’s in-house clinical team.

Goldman Sachs Alternatives Growth Equity

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

Grow Therapy

Why BHB is watching:

Goldman Sachs Alternatives Growth Equity’s portfolio company Grow Therapy made headlines earlier this year when it secured a whopping $150 million Series D round in March 2026. That brought the digital mental health platform’s projected annual revenue to more than $1 billion. Prior to the large capital round, Grow Therapy made a strategic investment and acquired the AI scribe tool Tenor Therapy in February. The company’s last funding round prior to its Series D was an $88 million Series C in 2024. The new infusion of capital, coupled with its latest acquisition, positions it to make additional, scalable investments going forward in the sector.

Kaiser Permanente Ventures

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

Headspace

Groups Recover Together

Mind 24-7

Noto (formerly NOCD)

Why BHB is watching:

Kaiser Permanente Ventures made BHB’s list of VC firms to watch in 2025, as well, but for different reasons. This year, the firm’s portfolio companies Headspace, Groups Recover Together and NOCD all were part of significant, strategic transactions.

Virtual mental health provider Headspace is set to be acquired by Sword Health in a cash deal reportedly valued at $300 million. The valuation is lower than some in the industry expected, particularly as many have had Headspace on their bingo cards as a company that could potentially IPO. The transaction comes just about one year after Headspace launched its direct-to-consumer therapy services. Sword Health, a New York City-based digital health provider, began making moves into behavioral health last summer and its valuation jumped to $4 billion. Sword Health’s CEO Virgilio Bento previously told HB that expanding capabilities into SMI care and growing its AI offerings, are part of its trajectory on its path toward a possible 2028 IPO.

Addiction treatment provider Groups Recover Together, another investment in Kaiser’s portfolio, made its first-ever acquisition in March 2026 and hinted that more activity in that vein is likely on the horizon. Its purchase of Better Life Partners deepens its resources throughout New England and introduces new care model elements that will allow the company to expand into new territories. Better Life Partners had been a bit of a distressed asset, with a series of financial and operational issues. Still, it had two assets that Groups wanted: virtual responsive care and walk-in clinic capabilities, CEO Cooper Zelnick, told BHB. Those are likely to scale further across the company over time.

Virtual OCD provider NOCD, another one of Kaiser’s portfolio companies, acquired trauma care provider Rebound Health earlier this year. Now the two entities operate under the new brand identity “Noto.” The transaction follows a market trend BHB has been keeping tabs on, where several new providers entering the market are entering niche areas of care and adding on, rather than starting broad and trying to narrow. The deal added trauma-focused care capabilities, which NOCD did not previously provide. An ongoing priority now for the newly formed company Noto is to continue to add new services for other complex behavioral health conditions.

General Catalyst

Why BHB is watching:

General Catalyst has long been a powerhouse investment firm known for backing successful healthcare companies with venture investments. Throughout 2026, several of its portfolio companies were part of sizable transactions or on the receiving end of large capital infusions.

Late last year, General Catalyst led a $50 million funding round for New York City-based Radial, which provides clinic-based interventional psychiatry services like transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Spravato, and neuromodulation treatments. Not only was the funding a vote of confidence from its investors, zooming out, interventional psychiatry is also on the rise across the industry as the latest hot commodity.

Following the $50 million Series A round, Radial acquired Mindful Health Solutions, a larger and older outpatient operator, this August for an undisclosed amount. Mindful Health Solutions has similar interventional psychiatry offerings and this single deal exponentially multiplied Radial’s geographic footprint. Radial is less than one year into its hold period with General Catalyst and anticipates tailwinds from the boom in interventional psychiatry will propel it further.

Also, as part of General Catalyst’s massive investment portfolio, Spring Health disclosed its plans to acquire digital mental health platform Alma in January. The transaction took place amid a wave of digital health dealmaking that began in 2026. Digital mental health is an area that is likely to continue to see consolidation following the explosion of solutions out of the pandemic, which is starting to balance out. Spring’s move to buy Alma skyrocketed its revenue expectations to $1 billion in its first year following the close of the deal, with its valuation rising to between $6 billion and $7 billion.

Other noteworthy developments among General Catalyst’s investments this year were also InStride Health’s $30 million Series C and Birches Health’s $20 million capital raise. Pediatric behavioral health provider InStride raised the capital at the beginning of 2026 and told BHB it plans to use it to expand into new markets. Birches Health’s funding came late in 2025, but has remained noteworthy in 2026, as both public and private audiences have renewed their attention on gambling addiction, which is one of its primary service lines. It’s likely there will be more expansion or consolidation in this area of behavioral and process addictions over time as concerns about gambling and social media rise.

HealthQuest Capital

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

AnswersNow

Why BHB is watching:

Virtual autism therapy provider AnswersNow secured a $40 million Series B in January, marking its first fundraise since 2023. The company provides ABA care via telehealth with board-certified behavior analysts (BCBAs), which is typically a clinic-based service. AnswersNow executives said that following the new capital infusion, its focus will be on “aggressively” scaling its platform, eventually adding new service lines and expanding its use of AI. HealthQuest Capital successfully exited AmWell, another behavioral health company, in the past.

data.title: Mental health utilization is up - but employer spending fell 7% in 2025
data.ai_summary: In 2025, 73% of large employers reported increased mental health and substance use disorder utilization, while average employer spending fell about 7% year over year. The gap between rising demand and falling investment is widening, and brokers are advised to evaluate network connectivity and outcomes data at renewal.
data.author: Mark Rosanes

industries.name: Behavioral Health Provider Network Management & Credentialing
Large Group Health Insurance (Mid-Market & National Accounts)

data.full_text:
The gap between rising demand and falling investment is widening, and brokers have a clear role at renewal Benefits By Mark Rosanes Aug 31, 2026 Share Seventy-three percent of large employers reported increased utilization of mental health and substance use disorder services in 2025, and another 17% expected demand to climb further, according to the Business Group on Health's 2026 Employer Health Care Strategy Survey. The problem for brokers helping clients navigate renewal is that employer spending on mental health resources moved in the opposite direction: NFP's 2026 US Benefits Trend Report found average spending fell roughly 7% year over year in 2025. That gap - rising demand, falling investment - is the central tension in employer mental health benefits right now, and it is shaping both the vendor landscape and the conversations brokers need to be having with clients before next renewal. Why access remains the core problem The treatment gap in the US sits in the background of every employer mental health conversation. SAMHSA's 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health found that 61.5 million adults - 23.4% of the US population - had any mental illness in 2024, but only about 52% received treatment. That leaves roughly 29.5 million adults with a diagnosable condition who received no care. Insurance coverage is a significant factor in whether people access care. Platforms built around insurance reimbursement - Grow Therapy, Headway, and Talkiatry - have scaled most rapidly by reducing the friction between a patient's coverage and an available in-network provider. Grow Therapy reported facilitating 7 million visits in 2025, raised a $150 million Series D in March at a $3 billion valuation, and stated coverage of 220 million insured Americans through partnerships with more than 125 health plans. That model - insurance-first, provider network at scale - is increasingly where the employer market is heading. The EAP model's structural limits The traditional employee assistance program (EAP) is where most employers currently anchor their mental health benefit, and utilization data suggests it is underperforming. A Prudential Group Insurance survey, cited in an August 2025 report, found that while 59% of employers offer EAPs, more than half of eligible employees have never used one. Barriers include concerns about confidentiality, uncertainty about what the program covers, and stigma. Industry estimates typically put annual EAP utilization at between 3% and 6% of eligible employees, though rates vary by employer size and program design. Low utilization conceals a downstream cost that brokers can make visible. An employee who does not use an EAP and whose mental health needs escalate will often surface in the claims data later through higher short-term disability costs, increased absenteeism, or more intensive health plan utilization. Brokers who can show employer clients the cost of untreated mental health conditions using their own claims data have a more concrete case for upgrading the benefit than engagement metrics alone provide. The shift in the vendor landscape reflects this pressure. Platforms like Lyra Health, Spring Health, and Modern Health have replaced or augmented traditional EAPs at a growing share of mid-market and enterprise employers, offering faster matching, more sessions, and measurable outcomes reporting. Spring Health reports engagement rates often ten times the traditional EAP average. What brokers need to evaluate at renewal Two structural questions now define the employer mental health benefit conversation at renewal. The first is whether the current offering connects to the health plan's behavioral health network, or runs beside it. An EAP that operates parallel to the health plan but does not hand off to in-network providers creates an access cliff - employees exhaust EAP sessions and then face the full barrier of finding in-network care on their own. Universal Health Services' $835 million acquisition of Talkspace, completed August 17, is a direct market response to that structural gap. It creates a referral pathway from virtual therapy through to inpatient behavioral health within a single organization, removing a coordination step that brokers and EAP administrators have typically had to handle manually. The second question is whether the employer can measure what the benefit is producing. Business Group on Health noted that with utilization rates now high, employers should shift focus from access to unit cost and quality, specifically whether employees are getting the right mental health support at the right time. More than half of eligible employees have never used their EAP, and the vendors gaining ground in 2026 are those providing employers with outcomes data rather than session counts alone. The employer mental health benefit is no longer a renewal checkbox. The data on rising utilization, falling investment, and a widening access gap creates a clear advisory opening. Audit what the client has, determine whether it connects to the health plan network, assess whether outcomes data is available, and use claims data to make the cost-of-inaction case. Employer health costs are on a 15-year high trajectory, and mental health utilization is now explicitly identified as a cost driver alongside GLP-1s and specialty drugs. Brokers who can frame the evaluation clearly for clients are better positioned heading into a difficult renewal environment. data.author: Nathaan Demers

industries.name: Behavioral Health for Children & Adolescents (Youth Services)

data.full_text:
Patience is not caution: The case for rethinking capital in youth mental health

With rates of anxiety and depression among young people near all-time highs, there is no shortage of founders working within the youth mental health space. And they are not short on innovation, passion or capabilities. However, the funding boom-bust cycle in the behavioral health sector following the influx of investment capital during COVID leaves many companies struggling to secure funding that is aligned with the nuances of innovation in a highly regulated, fragmented behavioral healthcare system. In prior clinical roles, I have supported hundreds of young people coping with mental health challenges and families navigating care systems with long waitlists and countless access barriers. The challenges felt tangible, human and present. Now, working at Hopelab in an impact investing capacity, I see a different systemic barrier — the mismatch between how early-stage mental health companies grow and how they’re funded. That mismatch shapes whether young people have access to the supports they need or are left without them. Boom and bust The behavioral health funding environment tells a stark story. Venture capital deployment peaked at roughly $5 billion in 2021 at the height of COVID, up from approximately $2 billion in 2020. Since then, investments have returned to 2020 levels and, according to some reports, have contracted further. While the causes are many, a key factor is the growth expectations associated with venture capital, which can be misaligned with the realities of early-stage behavioral health companies. From lengthy payor contracting cycles to the complexities of scaling clinical operations across state lines, early-stage growth in this space is time and resource intensive. As a result, much of the capital deployed from 2023 through the present has concentrated on later-stage companies — specifically high-margin service providers such as psychiatry — that have cleared early-stage growing pains and are ready for massive scale. For example, the telepsychiatry provider Talkiatry raised a $210 million Series D in February 2026. While that shift has expanded access to services for many in need, the challenge lies in the constriction of capital for early-stage companies innovating in the space, especially those serving traditionally underserved populations. Seeking patient capital The boom-bust cycle has left many early-stage companies caught between a rock and a hard place: either accepting venture capital that pushes for rapid scale before their care models, compliance infrastructure and reimbursement pathways are stable, or endlessly seeking a rare funding source that tolerates slower, evidence-driven growth. As a result, many run out of time and are forced to close their doors before achieving lasting impact and commercial success. Venture timelines reward velocity, not validation, and in behavioral health, that imbalance often derails both mission and business. Not all sectors are created equal. Tech-first companies like the newest email copilot or AI assistant can grow as fast as consumer markets allow, unencumbered by regulatory oversight, clinical safeguards and complex reimbursement models. Mental health innovators cannot — and should not — because the regulations in place serve an important purpose. But the industry’s highly regulated nature, spanning HIPAA compliance, data governance, licensure requirements and clinical supervision, means responsible scaling takes longer in the early stages than in other sectors. Rushing risks eroding clinical outcomes and consumer trust, both of which are essential to long-term viability for youth-serving behavioral health companies. But how do we — as investors and funders — change this dynamic? Based on primary research and conversations with colleagues and organizations across the field, we propose an alternative path: aligning funding timelines with market realities through more patient capital. Laying the groundwork for growth Patient capital gives youth-serving behavioral health companies the room to go deep within specific markets rather than reaching for wide geographic scale too early, providing the runway needed to become venture ready. By initially focusing within a state or several states, companies can build on a smaller set of clinical and operating regulations and demonstrate clinical outcomes, operational efficiency and financial performance under real-world conditions. With roughly 30 million youth on Medicaid in the United States, the reality is that many states have enough market share to prove out these models. As companies mature in these select markets, they can improve operational efficiency and margins, prioritizing new states with large target populations, favorable reimbursement rates and analogous regulations. This approach builds staying power rather than hype, fostering trust among consumers and buyers — and, in time, making these companies ready for the growth expectations of traditional venture. For example, Flourish Health, a company serving youth and young adults on Medicaid living with severe and persistent mental illnesses, just announced a $26 million Series A. Its growth model involved going deep within a select few markets in the early stage, allowing for the fine-tuning of clinical and operational efficiency, while also allowing enough time for evidence generation. In line with this growth trajectory, the company sought a bridge round that Hopelab co-led with Acumen America, with the understanding that funding was to be used for depth in existing markets, as opposed to scale, an approach less aligned with the orientation of traditional venture funds. Doing so afforded the company additional time and focus to establish a strong foundation and achieve margin expansion within Medicaid populations, which then positioned it to raise a large Series A focused on scale. An ask for investors It’s worth being honest: Not all companies innovating in any space are a fit for traditional venture capital, and the behavioral health field is no exception. However, that does not mean they are weak businesses that should not exist. The caveat is that many require capital that understands the nuances of the space in the early stages, giving them the time to become venture-ready before meeting the growth expectations of traditional venture capital. This is not a call for caution; patient capital is often mistaken for playing it safe, when in fact it is the de-risking work — proving outcomes, stabilizing reimbursement and building trust — that venture-scale growth depends on. Our ask for fellow investors and funders is specific: Consider co-investing in, or helping to create, patient and blended-capital models that bring together grants, philanthropic capital and other nondilutive funding for early-stage behavioral health companies. These instruments provide the runway required to drive innovation and outcomes — and ultimately to determine whether the young people and families I saw in clinical practice will have access to the supports they need. Speed is not synonymous with success. In youth mental health innovation, patience is not caution; it is a prerequisite for lasting impact. Nathaan Demers is principal investor at Hopelab. Guest posts on ImpactAlpha represent the opinions of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the views of ImpactAlpha.
